## Summary

When a streaming `chat.completions` request to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint returns **HTTP 200 but the SSE body yields zero usable chunks** (an empty stream, or a non-standard `error:` data frame that the OpenAI SDK doesn't surface as content), the streaming consumer in `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py` exits its loop with no content and `finish_reason = None`, and then **fabricates a successful empty `stop` turn** instead of raising. The agent accepts the empty turn (and can re-loop on a persistent condition), which presents to the user as a silent "stuck"/hung agent with no error surfaced.

## Where (function/symbols; line numbers approximate)

In `interruptible_streaming_api_call` (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py`):

- The consume loop `for chunk in stream:` (~L1758) exits normally on a zero-chunk stream — `content_parts`, `reasoning_parts`, and `tool_calls_acc` all stay empty and `finish_reason` stays `None`.
- When the mock response is assembled (~L1938): `effective_finish_reason = finish_reason or 'stop'` — this turns the empty/errored result into a valid-looking `stop` turn. No error is raised, so it never enters the retry/error path.

Related: the OpenAI-wire path has no stream-parse-error recognition equivalent to the Anthropic path (`run_agent.py` `_is_provider_stream_parse_error` only matches Anthropic's `"expected ident at line"`), so a malformed OpenAI-style stream is dropped silently rather than surfaced.

## Why it matters

Some OpenAI-compatible servers/proxies emit a `200` with an empty or non-standard-error SSE body under certain conditions (e.g. context overflow, or an upstream that returns an error inside a `data:` frame). Today that becomes an invisible empty assistant turn rather than a recoverable error, and on a persistent condition the agent can loop on empty turns.

## Proposed fix (provider-agnostic, defense-in-depth)

Add a **post-loop zero-chunk guard** just before the mock response is built (~L1900), so an empty result becomes a real, retryable error that flows through the existing retry/recovery machinery instead of a fabricated successful turn:

```python
if finish_reason is None and not content_parts and not reasoning_parts and not tool_calls_acc:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "Provider returned an empty stream with no finish_reason "
        "(possible upstream error or malformed SSE)."
    )
```

**Optional companion** — a first-token deadline (e.g. `HERMES_STREAM_FIRST_TOKEN_TIMEOUT`, default ~60s) enforced in the existing outer poll loop and **not** suppressed for local endpoints, to bound the *blocking*-empty case (stream opens but never emits a chunk). This matters for local endpoints in particular because the stale-stream detector is disabled for them (~L2299-2301) and the httpx read timeout is raised to the API timeout (~L1695-1696), leaving no short backstop. (For non-local endpoints the standard read timeout already bounds the blocking case, so the post-loop guard above is the key fix.)

## Repro sketch

Point Hermes at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that returns `HTTP 200` with an empty SSE body (or an `error:` frame) for some request, send a message, and observe the agent produce a silent empty turn / appear to hang, rather than surfacing an error or retrying.

## Impact

Low-risk, contained change in the streaming finalizer; turns a silent-empty-turn failure mode (which looks like a hang) into a normal recoverable error for any provider/proxy that emits a malformed or empty stream.

items.title: [Bug]:  `per-session compression lock` only prevents same-window concurrent fork, but not cross-turn stale-parent fork

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### Bug Description

The `per-session compression lock` (introduced to fix the Damien incident of 2026-05-28) successfully prevents two paths from concurrently compressing the same `session_id` in the same window. However, it does **not** prevent a stale parent from being compressed again in a later turn, leading to the same parent session ending up with multiple compression children.

**The gap**: if `review_agent` wins the compression race, its new child session is **not adopted by the gateway** — `background_review_callback` only sends a text summary, never propagates the new `session_id`. The gateway continues to point to the old parent, so the main agent starts the next foreground turn from the stale parent and can compress it again, creating a second sibling child.

Final lineage shape:

```
P (compression)
├─ W   (created by winner in Phase 1 — e.g. review_agent)
└─ M   (created later by main agent from stale P in Phase 2)
```

Both children are sibling compression continuations of the same parent, just produced at different times rather than concurrently.

### Steps to Reproduce

The following test can added to `tests/agent/test_compression_concurrent_fork.py` and **passes** (proving the defect exists):

```
def test_stale_parent_can_fork_again_after_lock_race(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    """Regression: per-session compression lock only prevents same-window
    concurrent fork — it does NOT prevent a stale parent from being
    compressed again in a later sequential call.

    Phase 1 (concurrent): two agents share parent_sid → one wins, one loses.
    Phase 2 (sequential): the loser (still holding parent_sid) compresses
    alone → creates a SECOND child from the same parent.

    Without cross-turn stale-parent protection the same parent ends up with
    two compression children.  This test is a defect reproduction — it
    SHOULD fail once canonical adoption or parent-rotated detection is
    implemented.
    """
    db = SessionDB(db_path=tmp_path / "state.db")

    parent_sid = "STALE_PARENT_REPRO"
    db.create_session(parent_sid, source="discord")

    agent_a = _build_agent_with_db(db, parent_sid)
    agent_b = _build_agent_with_db(db, parent_sid)
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": f"m{i}"} for i in range(20)]

    # ── Phase 1: concurrent compression race ─────────────────────────────
    def run(agent):
        try:
            agent._compress_context(messages, "sys", approx_tokens=120_000)
        except Exception:
            raise

    t_a = threading.Thread(target=run, args=(agent_a,), name="main_turn")
    t_b = threading.Thread(target=run, args=(agent_b,), name="review_fork")
    t_a.start()
    t_b.start()
    t_a.join(timeout=10)
    t_b.join(timeout=10)

    # Phase 1 assertions: exactly one winner, one loser, one child
    rotated = [a for a in (agent_a, agent_b) if a.session_id != parent_sid]
    not_rotated = [a for a in (agent_a, agent_b) if a.session_id == parent_sid]

    assert len(rotated) == 1, (
        f"Phase 1: expected exactly 1 winner, got {len(rotated)}"
    )
    assert len(not_rotated) == 1, (
        f"Phase 1: expected exactly 1 loser, got {len(not_rotated)}"
    )

    winner = rotated[0]
    loser = not_rotated[0]
    winner_sid = winner.session_id
    assert winner_sid != parent_sid
    assert loser.session_id == parent_sid

    rows_after_race = db._conn.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM sessions WHERE parent_session_id = ?",
        (parent_sid,),
    ).fetchall()
    assert len(rows_after_race) == 1, (
        f"Phase 1: expected 1 child, got {len(rows_after_race)}"
    )
    assert rows_after_race[0][0] == winner_sid, (
        f"Phase 1 child should be winner's new session_id"
    )

    # The lock must be released — loser can acquire next
    assert db.get_compression_lock_holder(parent_sid) is None, (
        "Lock leaked after Phase 1 — loser cannot re-compress"
    )

    # ── Phase 2: loser compresses again (sequential, no race) ────────────
    loser._compress_context(messages, "sys", approx_tokens=120_000)
    loser_sid = loser.session_id

    assert loser_sid != parent_sid, (
        f"Phase 2: loser ({loser_sid}) should have rotated away from "
        f"parent ({parent_sid})"
    )
    assert loser_sid != winner_sid, (
        f"Phase 2: loser's new session_id ({loser_sid}) collides with "
        f"winner's ({winner_sid}) — same child id for different parents "
        f"is astronomically unlikely; this is a UUID collision"
    )

    # ── Final state: same parent now has TWO children ───────────────────
    rows_final = db._conn.execute(
        "SELECT id, parent_session_id FROM sessions WHERE parent_session_id = ?",
        (parent_sid,),
    ).fetchall()

    assert len(rows_final) == 2, (
        f"DEFECT REPRODUCED: parent session has {len(rows_final)} children. "
        f"The per-session compression lock prevented concurrent fork "
        f"(Phase 1 ✓) but did NOT prevent the stale parent from being "
        f"compressed again later (Phase 2 ✗). "
        f"Child sessions: {[r[0] for r in rows_final]}"
    )
    assert {row[0] for row in rows_final} == {winner_sid, loser_sid}, (
        f"Expected children {{{winner_sid}, {loser_sid}}}, "
        f"got {{{', '.join(row[0] for row in rows_final)}}}"
    )
```

### Expected Behavior

If a compression winner already created a continuation child from parent `P`, later paths should **not** be able to create another compression child from the same `P`

### Actual Behavior

- Concurrent double-rotation is prevented ✓
- But if `review_agent` wins, its child is not adopted by gateway
- The foreground path continues from stale parent `P` on the next turn
- `P` can be compressed again → second child created
- Same parent ends up with multiple children (just not concurrently)


### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
NA
```

### Operating System

mac OS 15.5

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.15.1

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

_No response_

### Proposed Fix (optional)

### disable compression on `review_agent` (simplest)

The only two paths that share a `session_id` and can race on compression are the main agent and the `review_agent`. The `review_agent` is single-lifecycle (daemon thread, one `run_conversation()` call then dead), and its job — reviewing the conversation to update memory/skills — requires full context. Compression would strip detail and degrade review quality.

Either race outcome leaves the main agent's flow intact:
- Main wins → review skips compression, proceeds with review, finishes lifecycle
- Review wins → main skips compression, compresses again on the next turn and updates gateway session_id; review's new session_id dies with the review lifecycle

Therefore, **simply preventing `review_agent` from triggering compression eliminates the race entirely**, and the `per-session compression lock` becomes unnecessary complexity.

**Change**: `agent/background_review.py`, after `review_agent` construction (around line 451, after `review_agent.session_id = agent.session_id`), add:

```python
review_agent.compression_enabled = False
```

Why this works:
- Both compression trigger points in `agent/conversation_loop.py:598` (preflight) and `:4046` (mid-loop) gate on `agent.compression_enabled` first
- Setting it to `False` short-circuits both paths — no compression call, no race, no orphan child

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: fix(feishu): remove outdated markdown table fallback, always use post format
items.body:
# Issue 内容 (复制到 https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/new)

## 标题
fix(feishu): remove outdated markdown table fallback, always use post format

## 正文

### Problem

When Hermes sends Markdown messages containing pipe tables to Feishu, the message content is displayed as raw Markdown source code instead of rendered output.

### Root Cause

In `gateway/platforms/feishu.py`, the `_build_outbound_payload()` method has an outdated fallback logic that detects pipe tables via `_MARKDOWN_TABLE_RE` and forces the message type to `text` (plain text):

```python
if _MARKDOWN_TABLE_RE.search(content):
    text_payload = {"text": content}
    return "text", json.dumps(text_payload, ensure_ascii=False)
```

This was originally a workaround for an older Feishu version where the Post format with `"tag": "md"` elements did not support tables. Feishu now supports all Markdown syntax natively in Post format.

### Fix

Always use Feishu's Post format (`msg_type: "post"`) with `{"tag": "md"}` elements for all outbound messages:

```python
def _build_outbound_payload(self, content: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    # Feishu post-type 'md' elements now natively support all markdown
    # syntax including pipe tables, code blocks, headings, etc.
    # Always use post format for proper markdown rendering.
    return "post", _build_markdown_post_payload(content)
```

This removes the `_MARKDOWN_TABLE_RE` fallback check and the plain-text fallback, ensuring all Markdown content (tables, headings, code blocks, lists, etc.) is properly rendered by Feishu.

### Testing

The fix has been applied locally and works with Hermes Agent v0.15.1. Gateway restart required after patch.

### Related

- File: `gateway/platforms/feishu.py` lines 4310-4320
- Regex: `_MARKDOWN_TABLE_RE` (line 159), `_MARKDOWN_HINT_RE` (line 153)

---

# PR 分支 (本地已备好，如需提交)

```bash
# 在 hermes-agent 目录下操作
git checkout fix/feishu-md-rendering

# 如果之后有了有权限的 token:
# gh pr create --repo NousResearch/hermes-agent \
#   --head bigsinger:fix/feishu-md-rendering \
#   --base main \
#   --title "fix(feishu): remove outdated markdown table fallback, always use post format" \
#   --body "同上 Issue 正文"
```

items.title: Cron one-shot whose script kills the gateway re-fires forever (no pre-run dispatch guard)
items.body:
## Summary

A one-shot cron job (`schedule.kind == "once"`, `repeat: {times: 1, completed: 0}`) whose `script` terminates the gateway process causes an **infinite restart loop**. The job never gets marked complete, so it re-fires on every gateway relaunch — sending the user a startup/shutdown notification each cycle (~10-15s apart).

Hit this in production on a macOS launchd-supervised gateway (away-node, no human at the machine). A leftover `no_agent` one-shot ran a script that did `launchctl kickstart -k gui/<uid>/ai.hermes.gateway` (intended as a one-time WhatsApp-bridge reload). The kickstart killed the gateway *before* the tick could record completion → loop.

## Root cause

`cron/jobs.py::mark_job_run()` is the function that increments `repeat.completed` and removes a one-shot once `completed >= times` (lines ~913-924). It is called **after** the job's script/agent finishes:

```python
# cron/jobs.py ~913
if job.get("repeat"):
    job["repeat"]["completed"] = job["repeat"].get("completed", 0) + 1
    times = job["repeat"].get("times")
    completed = job["repeat"]["completed"]
    if times is not None and times > 0 and completed >= times:
        jobs.pop(i)          # <-- only reached if we get here at all
        save_jobs(jobs)
        return
```

For a `no_agent` job the tick runs **inside** the gateway process. If the script kills the gateway, the tick dies before `mark_job_run` runs. The completion write never lands. On the next launchd `KeepAlive` relaunch the scheduler sees an enabled, past-due, never-completed one-shot and dispatches it again. Repeat forever.

This is at-least-once execution with the commit point *after* the side effect. Any abrupt tick death has the same effect (OOM, segfault, hard-timeout kill, panic) — gateway-suicide is just the most reliable trigger.

## Repro

1. Create a no_agent one-shot whose script kills the gateway:
   ```bash
   # ~/.hermes/scripts/suicide.sh
   launchctl kickstart -k "gui/$(id -u)/ai.hermes.gateway"
   ```
2. `hermes cron create "<past-or-now timestamp>" --script suicide.sh --no-agent` (one-shot, repeat times=1).
3. Gateway is launchd/systemd-supervised with KeepAlive.
4. Observe: gateway connects, ~10s later receives SIGTERM, KeepAlive relaunches, job fires again. `repeat.completed` stays `0` in `~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json`. User gets a notification per cycle.

Workaround once you're in it: `hermes cron remove <id>` (NOT `gateway stop/start` — the job re-fires on the next relaunch).

## Proposed fix

Make one-shot completion crash-safe by committing the dispatch **before** running the side effect, so a job can fire at most `times` times regardless of how the tick dies.

Preferred: a **pre-run attempt/dispatch counter** with `repeat.times` as a hard cap.
- Before invoking the script/agent, atomically increment a `repeat.dispatched` (or reuse `completed` as an at-most-once claim) under `_jobs_file_lock` and persist.
- Treat `times` as max-dispatch, not max-success. A job whose runtime self-destructs then fires at most N times instead of infinitely.
- Keep `mark_job_run` for status/last_error, but the removal/limit decision keys off the pre-run claim.

This bounds the blast radius for **every** mid-tick death, not just gateway-kills.

(Considered and rejected: greping the script text for gateway-kill verbs at create-time — brittle, easy to bypass via indirection, false-positives on comments, and doesn't cover the other ways a tick can die. The bug is the execution semantics, not the script content.)

Optionally, also warn at `cron create` time if a `no_agent` script appears to restart/kill the gateway, as a secondary nicety — but the durable fix is the pre-run commit.

## Environment
- Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29), macOS, launchd-supervised gateway, `no_agent` one-shot.

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main

items.body:
# [Bug] Windows Discord `/restart` stops Scheduled Task gateway but does not reliably relaunch it

## Bug Description

On native Windows, when the Hermes gateway is running under the Windows Scheduled Task install path, invoking `/restart` from Discord can shut the gateway down cleanly but fail to bring it back up. The gateway stays offline until the user physically accesses the Windows machine and runs `hermes gateway restart` from an external shell.

This is distinct from the already-reported “no Scheduled Task installed” case: in this case the Scheduled Task exists, `hermes gateway status` reports it, and the gateway process is running before the Discord `/restart` command.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On Windows, install/start the gateway via the Windows Scheduled Task path.
2. Confirm the gateway is running:
   ```text
   ✓ Scheduled Task registered: Hermes_Gateway
     Status: Running
     Last Run Time: 6/4/2026 1:10:15 AM
     Last Run Result: 267009
   ✓ Gateway process running (PID: 9192)
   ```
3. From Discord, invoke the gateway restart command, e.g. `/restart`.
4. Observe the gateway logs.
5. Try messaging the Discord bot again.

## Expected Behavior

Discord `/restart` should perform a full restart:

1. acknowledge the restart command
2. drain/stop the old gateway process
3. trigger an external Windows-safe restart path before or during shutdown
4. verify that the replacement gateway process is running
5. optionally send the usual restart notification after startup

The user should not need to open PowerShell on the Windows host to recover the bot.

## Actual Behavior

The gateway receives the Discord `/restart`, shuts down cleanly, but does not reliably relaunch. The Discord bot goes offline/unresponsive until the user manually runs:

```powershell
hermes gateway restart
```

Representative logs from a real occurrence:

```text
2026-06-04 01:05:37,399 INFO hermes_plugins.discord_platform.adapter: [Discord] slash '/restart' invoked by user=... id=... channel=... guild=...
2026-06-04 01:05:37,845 INFO gateway.run: Stopping gateway for restart...
2026-06-04 01:05:37,890 INFO gateway.run: Gateway stopped (total teardown 0.05s)
2026-06-04 01:10:17,709 INFO gateway.run: Starting Hermes Gateway...
2026-06-04 01:10:21,692 INFO gateway.run: Sent restart notification to discord:...
```

The ~5 minute gap was recovery after manual intervention from the Windows machine.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 / kernel version `10.0.26200` (Python `platform.platform()` reports `Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0`, but build >= 22000 maps to Windows 11)
- Hermes: `v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)`
- Python: `3.11.15`
- Gateway manager: Windows Scheduled Task
- Scheduled Task name: `Hermes_Gateway`
- Messaging platform: Discord

## Related Issues / Possible Duplicates

Related but not exact:

- #32779 — `/restart` silently fails on Windows when **no Scheduled Task is installed**. This issue differs because the Scheduled Task is installed and visible in `hermes gateway status`.
- #36213 — Windows `hermes gateway restart` does not verify old process termination, causing silent gateway failure. This is related to Windows restart robustness, but this report is specifically about Discord/gateway-initiated `/restart` under Scheduled Task leaving the bot down until an external shell restart.
- #38134 — Desktop update should auto-restart messaging gateway after update completes. Similar “gateway stays down until manual restart” UX, different trigger.

## Suspected Root Cause

The Discord `/restart` path is initiated inside the gateway process that is about to exit. On Windows, the Scheduled Task acts more like a launcher than a true process supervisor. A clean gateway exit does not necessarily cause the Scheduled Task to respawn the process.

There is also a CLI safety guard that prevents calling `hermes gateway restart` from inside the gateway process:

```text
Refusing to restart the gateway from inside the gateway process.
This command was blocked to prevent restart loops.
Use `hermes gateway restart` from a shell outside the running gateway.
```

That guard makes sense, but it leaves `/restart` needing a Windows-specific external restart helper that is launched before the old gateway exits.

## Proposed Fix

For Windows gateway-initiated restart requests:

1. Detect Windows + Scheduled Task install when `/restart` is invoked from a messaging platform.
2. Launch an external detached restart helper before stopping the gateway, or trigger the Scheduled Task in a way that does not depend on the dying gateway process.
3. The helper should:
   - wait for the old gateway PID to exit
   - force-kill only if needed after a timeout
   - start the Scheduled Task / detached `pythonw.exe` gateway process
   - verify the new gateway process is healthy
   - log failures clearly
4. Avoid routing through the generic `hermes gateway restart` command when `_HERMES_GATEWAY=1`, since that path intentionally refuses self-restart.

## Workaround

From a local shell on the Windows host, run:

```powershell
hermes gateway restart
```

This works because it is launched outside the gateway process, so it can safely stop the old gateway and start a replacement.

## Impact

This makes remote administration unreliable: the user can ask Octo/Hermes to restart from Discord, but if the restart path fails, the bot is unreachable until the user physically or remotely accesses the Windows PC and runs the restart command manually.

items.title: fix(compression): eliminate session duplication -- adopt in-place compaction like Claude Code and Codex

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Problem

Every time Hermes compresses context, it creates a **new session** chained via `parent_session_id`. This spawns duplicate entries in the WebUI sidebar (`My Chat`, `My Chat #2`, `My Chat #3`, etc.) for a single conversation. Over time this accumulates hundreds of orphan child sessions in `state.db`.

This is not how other agentic coding tools handle it, and it causes a cascade of downstream bugs:

- #33618 -- /goal lost after compression rotates session_id
- #34089 -- session ID desync between agent and gateway after split
- #25921 -- infinite preflight compression loop from reusing parent history
- #14238 -- pending response lost at session split boundary
- #33907 -- orphan sessions missing from state.db
- #36777 -- TUI session.info doesn't update after compression fork

## How Claude Code and Codex solve this

**Both tools keep the same session/thread ID for the entire conversation.** Compression never creates a new session.

### Claude Code (Anthropic Messages API)

- Single `session_id` for the entire conversation. No `parent_session_id` field exists in the schema.
- When context fills up, Claude Code calls the API with `context_management` containing a `compact_20260112` strategy.
- The API handles it server-side: summarizes old messages into a `compaction` content block, returns it alongside the response.
- Client appends the compaction block to the messages array and keeps going in the **same session**.
- All messages before the latest compaction block are transparently ignored by the API on subsequent requests.
- Evidence: 9,131 sessions in a Claude Code install, none with parent chains. Longest session has 4,033 messages in a single session_id.

### Codex (OpenAI Responses API)

- Single `thread_id` for the entire conversation. No `parent_thread_id` field (only `thread_spawn_edges` for actual subagent delegation).
- When context fills up, Codex calls the API with `compact_threshold` set.
- The API returns a `compaction` item that the client appends to the conversation.
- Everything before the compaction item gets dropped on the next request.
- Thread ID stays the same forever. Sessions with 500M+ tokens exist as single rows in the `threads` table.
- Compaction blobs are AES-encrypted server-side so the client never even sees the summary text.

### Key Insight

Both tools leverage their provider's **native server-side compaction API**. The provider returns a compaction artifact that the client injects into the message stream. The session/thread ID never changes.

## Proposed Fix

Hermes should adopt in-place compaction for **all models**, not just providers with native compaction APIs.

### For providers with native compaction (Anthropic, OpenAI)

Use the provider's built-in compaction API (Claude's `context_management`, OpenAI's `compact_threshold`). This is the ideal path -- the provider handles summarization and the client just manages message truncation. Zero custom summarization logic needed.

### For providers without native compaction (z.ai/GLM, Google, etc.)

Replicate the same pattern in client code:

1. **Generate summary** -- use the model to summarize the conversation history (similar to what Hermes already does in `conversation_compression.py`)
2. **Inject summary as a system message** -- prepend a compaction block to the messages array
3. **Truncate old messages** -- drop all messages before the summary block from the in-memory messages array
4. **Keep the same session_id** -- do NOT end the session, do NOT create a new session row, do NOT set `end_reason="compression"`, do NOT chain via `parent_session_id`
5. **Continue conversation** -- the next user message appends after the summary block as normal

### Config changes

Add a new option to control the strategy:

```yaml
compression:
  enabled: true
  threshold: 0.95
  mode: inplace  # "inplace" (default, no session split) | "split" (legacy, creates new session)
```

This preserves backward compat if anyone relies on the split behavior, but defaults to the new in-place approach.

### What changes in the code

In `conversation_compression.py`, the `compress_context` function currently:

```
1. Generate summary
2. end_session(end_reason="compression")
3. create_session(title=f"{title} #{n}", parent_session_id=old_id)
4. Reset flush cursors
```

It should instead:

```
1. Generate summary (existing logic, keep this)
2. Inject summary as system message at start of messages array
3. Truncate all messages before the summary
4. Update session title if desired (same session_id)
5. Continue in the same session
```

Lines 381-396 (the session split logic) get replaced with the in-place truncation. Everything else (summary generation, threshold calculation, protection of recent messages) stays the same.

### Schema changes

- `parent_session_id` column becomes unused for compression. Can be deprecated or kept for backward compat with existing session chains.
- No new columns needed. The same `messages` storage in the session works -- compaction is just another set of messages in the array.

## Benefits

1. **No more duplicate sessions** -- one conversation = one session row in the DB, from first message to last
2. **Fixes all related bugs** -- session ID desync, goal loss, preflight loops, orphan sessions, gateway desync all become impossible since the session_id never changes mid-conversation
3. **Cleaner WebUI** -- sidebar shows actual conversations, not chains of numbered copies
4. **Simpler state management** -- no parent_session_id lineage to track, no session chain queries needed
5. **Consistent with industry standard** -- Claude Code and Codex both work this way
6. **No data loss** -- compaction summaries are preserved as messages in the session, not lost when old sessions get pruned

## Environment

- Hermes v0.14.0
- Claude Code v2.1.143 (for reference behavior)
- Codex CLI v0.130.0 (for reference behavior)

items.title: [Bug]: Root package.json workspaces glob unconditionally pulls apps/desktop (and bootstrap-installer) into every unscoped npm command
items.body:
### Bug Description

Bug Description
The root package.json declares:

```json
"workspaces": [
  "apps/*",
  "ui-tui",
  "ui-tui/packages/*",
  "web"
]
```

Because of the apps/* glob, any command run from the repository root (npm audit, npm audit fix, npm install, npm ls, npm outdated, etc.) causes npm to resolve the entire workspace graph. This always materializes apps/desktop (Electron + node-pty@1.1.0) and apps/bootstrap-installer, even when the user only cares about the web UI, TUI, or is just running routine maintenance commands.

This is the core architectural problem. Related recent issues (#38358, #38311) are symptoms of it.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Clone/checkout the hermes-agent repo.
2. From the repo root, run:
```bash
npm ls --depth=0
```
(or npm audit, npm audit fix, npm install --package-lock-only, etc.)
3. Observe that the output includes the full apps/desktop tree (hermes@0.15.1 -> ./apps/desktop, node-pty, electron, etc.).
4. Compare with:
```bash
npm ls --workspaces=false --depth=0
```
This only shows the two tiny root dependencies.

5. On a minimal Linux environment (no build-essential), npm audit fix (or plain npm install) fails with:

```
gyp ERR! stack Error: not found: make
...
path /.../node_modules/node-pty
command sh -c node scripts/prebuild.js || node-gyp rebuild
```

(node-pty ships no Linux prebuilds; the install script always falls back to node-gyp.)

Alternatively, on an existing updated Hermes-Agent install, do a `hermes doctor && npm audit fix`

### Expected Behavior

- Running npm audit fix, npm audit, or similar at the root for web/TUI work should only resolve the relevant workspaces (or at minimum not force native rebuilds for desktop).
- The monorepo should support "light" root-level npm operations without pulling the full desktop/Electron dependency tree.
- Scoping (--workspace web, --workspaces=false) should be the documented/encouraged default for non-desktop tasks, or the structure should make accidental full resolution harder.


### Actual Behavior

Plain root npm commands always resolve everything via the single lockfile + workspaces declaration. This pulls ~200MB+ of Electron + forces Linux users to have make/g++/etc. installed just to run security updates or dependency hygiene commands. Installer scripts and some internal hermes_cli paths already work around this with explicit scoping, but direct developer usage and some code paths do not.


### Affected Component

Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Report       https://paste.rs/pw1Bx
agent.log    https://paste.rs/afvf7
gateway.log  https://paste.rs/RdDHG
```

### Operating System

Debian 13.4

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

0.15.1 (2026.5.29)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The single root package.json uses a broad apps/* glob for convenience (desktop dev gets automatic linking via the shared lockfile — see apps/desktop/README.md and apps/desktop/scripts/assert-root-install.cjs).

npm's workspace resolution has no "opt-out" at the command line for users who just want to run npm audit fix. Several mitigations exist in the tree:
- scripts/install.sh / install.ps1 deliberately do selective workspace installs for the browser-only path.
- Some functions in hermes_cli/main.py (e.g. _update_node_dependencies) already pass --workspace.
- But npm commands executed directly by developers (or slipped paths like the one in #38358) bypass this.

node-pty@1.1.0 (in apps/desktop/package.json) has no Linux prebuilts, so the fallback to node-gyp rebuild makes the problem painful on Linux.


### Proposed Fix (optional)

Options to discuss:
1. Change the workspaces declaration to list packages explicitly (exclude apps/desktop and apps/bootstrap-installer from the default glob) and update desktop dev instructions + linking logic.
2. Add root-level helper scripts (npm run install:web, npm run audit:web, etc.) that wrap scoped commands.
3. Make more (or all) internal npm calls in hermes_cli/ use --workspaces=false + explicit --workspace flags where appropriate (see the fix in PR for #38358).
4. Add prominent warnings in AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and the desktop README about the implications of root npm commands.
5. Explore whether desktop can be linked without being part of the root workspaces (separate lockfile? postinstall hook? etc.).

Related issues (symptoms of the same root cause):
- #38358 (missing --workspace web in _build_web_ui causing hermes update to pull desktop)
- #38311 (node-pty + missing make during install/update on Linux/WSL)


### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: [Bug]: Codex app-server sessions ignore configured/session cwd and start sandbox in Hermes home
items.body:
## Bug Description

Codex app-server runtime sessions can spawn from the Hermes daemon's process cwd instead of the configured gateway cwd or ACP/editor session cwd.

In my case the Hermes config had:

```yaml
terminal:
  cwd: /home/jplew/Sites/myproject
  docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace: true
```

and Codex config trusted the same project:

```toml
default_permissions = ":workspace"

[projects."/home/jplew/Sites/myproject"]
trust_level = "trusted"
```

However, a new Codex runtime session launched through the gateway still reported this environment context:

```text
<cwd>/home/jplew/.hermes</cwd>
...
<workspace_roots><root>/home/jplew/.hermes</root></workspace_roots>
...
<entry access="write"><path>/home/jplew/.hermes</path></entry>
```

As a result, Codex could read files broadly but could only write under `/home/jplew/.hermes` and `/tmp`. Writes to the intended project directory `/home/jplew/Sites/myproject` required escalation or failed under the managed sandbox.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes gateway or ACP with a project cwd that is not the Hermes home directory:

   ```yaml
   terminal:
     cwd: /home/jplew/Sites/myproject
     docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace: true
   ```

2. Use the OpenAI Codex app-server runtime through ACP:

   ```yaml
   model:
     provider: openai-codex
     openai_runtime: codex_app_server
   ```

3. Start/restart the Hermes gateway and create a new Codex runtime session, or create a new ACP/Codex session from an editor workspace.

4. Ask Codex to inspect its environment or attempt a write probe under the configured cwd:

   ```sh
   printf 'probe\n' > /home/jplew/Sites/myproject/.codex-write-probe
   ```

5. Observe that the Codex runtime's `cwd` and writable workspace root are the Hermes home directory rather than the configured/session cwd.

## Expected Behavior

Codex app-server sessions should start from the active Hermes working directory:

- Gateway/messaging sessions should use `terminal.cwd` as bridged to `TERMINAL_CWD`.
- ACP/editor sessions should use the ACP session cwd.

For the example above, Codex should receive `/home/jplew/Sites/myproject` as its cwd/workspace root, so workspace-scoped permissions allow normal project writes there.

## Actual Behavior

Hermes terminal/file tools resolve the configured/session cwd correctly, but the Codex app-server runtime can be spawned with the Hermes daemon process cwd.

The Codex environment context shows:

```text
cwd: /home/jplew/.hermes
writable root: /home/jplew/.hermes
```

instead of:

```text
cwd: /home/jplew/Sites/myproject
writable root: /home/jplew/Sites/myproject
```

This prevents Codex from writing to the intended workspace under normal workspace permissions.

## Affected Component

- Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)
- Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)
- Configuration (config.yaml, .env, hermes setup)

More specifically: Codex app-server cwd resolution in gateway sessions, plus ACP session creation for editor sessions.

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

- Telegram

The latest real-session reproduction was observed through Telegram/gateway. The same underlying Codex app-server fallback also affects ACP unless ACP stamps the session cwd onto the agent.

## Debug Report

Not uploaded yet.

Local details:

```text
Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)
Project: /home/jplew/.hermes/hermes-agent
Python: 3.11.15
OpenAI SDK: 2.24.0
Up to date
Branch: reference-images-for-image-gen
Commit: e8a865f53
```

## Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS

```text
Linux jplew 6.8.0-124-generic #124-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Tue May 26 13:00:45 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

## Python Version

```text
Python 3.11.15
```

## Hermes Version

```text
Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)
```

## Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

There is no Python traceback. The visible failure mode is the Codex runtime environment context and sandbox permissions:

```text
<cwd>/home/jplew/.hermes</cwd>
<workspace_roots><root>/home/jplew/.hermes</root></workspace_roots>
<entry access="write"><path>/home/jplew/.hermes</path></entry>
```

Attempting to write to `/home/jplew/Sites/myproject` from the Codex runtime failed under the managed sandbox:

```text
/bin/bash: line 2: /home/jplew/Sites/myproject/.codex-write-probe: Read-only file system
```

Writing under `/home/jplew/.hermes` succeeded, confirming the sandbox was scoped to the daemon cwd rather than the intended project.

Gateway logs showed the configured `terminal.cwd` was present in `config.yaml`, but Codex app-server still started with the daemon cwd:

```text
agent.transports.codex_app_server_session: codex app-server thread started: ... cwd=/home/jplew/.hermes
```

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

There are two related cwd propagation gaps.

For ACP/editor sessions, `acp_adapter/session.py` correctly stores the ACP cwd in `SessionState.cwd` and calls `_register_task_cwd(session_id, cwd)`, which makes regular Hermes terminal/file tools resolve the session cwd correctly.

However, `_make_agent()` did not stamp the cwd onto the `AIAgent` instance as `agent.session_cwd`.

The Codex app-server runtime later uses this field when lazily spawning the app-server session:

```python
# agent/codex_runtime.py
cwd = getattr(agent, "session_cwd", None) or os.getcwd()
agent._codex_session = CodexAppServerSession(
    cwd=cwd,
    approval_callback=approval_callback,
)
```

Because ACP-created agents did not have `session_cwd`, the Codex runtime fell back to `os.getcwd()`.

For gateway/messaging sessions, there is no ACP `session_cwd` to stamp. Hermes already bridges `terminal.cwd` into `TERMINAL_CWD`, and other runtime/tool surfaces use `agent.runtime_cwd.resolve_agent_cwd()` to honor that. The Codex app-server path missed that helper and fell back directly to `os.getcwd()`, which in gateway/daemon context is the Hermes home/install directory.

## Proposed Fix (optional)

Fix both paths:

1. After constructing the ACP `AIAgent`, set:

```python
agent.session_cwd = cwd
```

in `acp_adapter/session.py::_make_agent()`, before the first Codex app-server turn can lazily spawn.

2. In `agent/codex_runtime.py`, resolve the Codex app-server cwd as:

```python
from agent.runtime_cwd import resolve_agent_cwd

cwd = getattr(agent, "session_cwd", None) or str(resolve_agent_cwd())
```

This preserves ACP `session_cwd` precedence while making gateway/messaging sessions honor `TERMINAL_CWD`.

Regression tests:

- Stub `run_agent.AIAgent` and assert that `SessionManager(...).create_session(cwd="/tmp/project").agent.session_cwd == "/tmp/project"`.
- Set `TERMINAL_CWD` in a Codex app-server runtime test and assert `CodexAppServerSession` receives that path when `agent.session_cwd` is absent.

Local verification:

```text
python -m pytest tests/acp/test_session.py -q
42 passed, 1 warning

python -m pytest tests/run_agent/test_codex_app_server_integration.py -q
16 passed, 1 warning
```

## Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: Cron ticker waits for all due jobs, so one long active job can starve later schedules
items.body:
## Summary

The gateway cron ticker calls `cron_tick()` synchronously and `cron/scheduler.py::tick()` waits for every due job future before returning. Because cron agent runs are explicitly allowed to run for hours while active, one long active job can prevent the ticker from discovering and dispatching later due jobs.

## Evidence

Local checkout: `/srv/platform/link_dot_hermes/hermes-agent`.

- `gateway/run.py:18299-18303` runs the cron tick directly in the ticker loop:

```py
while not stop_event.is_set():
    try:
        cron_tick(verbose=False, adapters=adapters, loop=loop)
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:1999-2007` submits due jobs and then waits for every future with `as_completed(..., timeout=600)` before `tick()` can return:

```py
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=_max_workers) as _tick_pool:
    _futures = []
    for job in parallel_jobs:
        _ctx = contextvars.copy_context()
        _futures.append(_tick_pool.submit(_ctx.run, _process_job, job))
    for f in concurrent.futures.as_completed(_futures, timeout=600):
        _results.append(f.result())
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:1658-1661` documents that agent jobs may run for hours as long as they stay active:

```py
# Run the agent with an *inactivity*-based timeout: the job can run
# for hours if it's actively calling tools / receiving stream tokens,
```

## Impact

A single long-running but healthy cron job can block the gateway cron ticker. Jobs due while it is still running are not claimed or dispatched until the previous tick returns. This is high impact for watchdogs, alerting jobs, and recurring operational automation, where one large research/report job can delay unrelated monitoring or recovery jobs for hours.

The `as_completed(..., timeout=600)` also conflicts with the "can run for hours" contract: once the timeout is hit, the iterator raises, and the executor context manager can still wait for running futures while the gateway only logs a debug-level cron tick error.

## Proposed change

Split due-job claiming from job completion:

1. On each tick, claim/lease due jobs and compute their next-run/dispatch state under lock.
2. Dispatch jobs to a persistent scheduler executor or task registry.
3. Return immediately so later ticks can keep discovering due work.
4. Use completion callbacks to save output, deliver, and finalize `mark_job_run()` state.
5. Add lease expiry/recovery for gateway restart or worker crash.

A minimal mitigation would be to keep an in-process in-flight set and avoid waiting for all job futures in the gateway ticker.

## Verification

- Add a regression test or integration harness with:
  - Job A: active long-running cron job lasting >10 minutes.
  - Job B: short job due one minute after Job A starts.
- Before the fix, Job B does not run until Job A completes or the blocked tick exits.
- After the fix, Job B runs at its scheduled time while Job A remains active.
- Verify watchdog-style jobs continue firing while unrelated long jobs are in flight.

items.title: Cron standalone delivery has no timeout, so hung platform sends block job finalization
items.body:
## Summary

Cron live-adapter delivery has explicit timeouts, but the standalone delivery fallback awaits `_send_to_platform()` through `asyncio.run(coro)` with no timeout. If a platform send hangs, `_process_job()` never reaches `mark_job_run()`, leaving scheduler state unfinalized and potentially blocking the whole cron tick.

## Evidence

Local checkout: `/srv/platform/link_dot_hermes/hermes-agent`.

- `cron/scheduler.py:733-736` uses an explicit timeout for the live-adapter path:

```py
send_result = future.result(timeout=60)
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:780-784` runs standalone delivery without any timeout:

```py
coro = _send_to_platform(platform, pconfig, chat_id, cleaned_delivery_content, thread_id=thread_id, media_files=media_files)
try:
    result = asyncio.run(coro)
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:791-793` only applies a timeout in the nested RuntimeError/thread fallback, not the normal standalone path:

```py
future = pool.submit(asyncio.run, _send_to_platform(...))
result = future.result(timeout=30)
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:1952-1967` calls `mark_job_run()` only after delivery returns:

```py
if should_deliver:
    delivery_error = _deliver_result(job, deliver_content, adapters=adapters, loop=loop)
...
mark_job_run(job["id"], success, error, delivery_error=delivery_error)
```

## Impact

A network/API hang in standalone platform delivery can keep a cron job in limbo after execution. The output may already be saved, but repeat counts, status, `last_run_at`, next-run recomputation, and `last_delivery_error` are not finalized. Since the current tick waits for `_process_job()`, the same hang can also block unrelated due jobs.

This is a scheduler lifecycle and operational reliability risk, especially for long-running autonomous jobs that deliver to Telegram/Discord/etc. outside a live adapter path.

## Proposed change

- Wrap the normal standalone send in an explicit timeout, for example:

```py
result = asyncio.run(asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=60))
```

- Apply equivalent timeout handling to all fallback send paths.
- On timeout, set `delivery_error` and continue to `mark_job_run()` so job state advances and operators can see the failed delivery.
- Consider a per-platform or per-job delivery timeout setting.

## Verification

- Monkeypatch `_send_to_platform()` to `await asyncio.sleep(9999)`.
- Run a due cron job with standalone delivery enabled.
- Before the fix, `_deliver_result()` / `tick()` hangs and `mark_job_run()` is not reached.
- After the fix, delivery times out, `last_delivery_error` records the timeout, and scheduling continues.

items.title: Cron live-adapter media delivery failures are swallowed as successful deliveries
items.body:
## Summary

Cron delivery extracts `MEDIA:/path` attachments and sends them through the live gateway adapter after the text message succeeds. If the media send fails, `_send_media_via_adapter()` only logs a warning and returns no error, so the cron job is marked as successfully delivered with no `last_delivery_error`.

## Evidence

Local checkout: `/srv/platform/link_dot_hermes/hermes-agent`.

- `cron/scheduler.py:604-615` catches media-send failures and only logs warnings:

```py
try:
    result = future.result(timeout=30)
except TimeoutError:
    future.cancel()
    raise
if result and not getattr(result, "success", True):
    logger.warning("Job '%s': media send failed ...")
except Exception as e:
    logger.warning("Job '%s': failed to send media ...")
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:759-773` marks the live-adapter delivery successful when the text send succeeded, even after media send warnings:

```py
if adapter_ok and media_files:
    _send_media_via_adapter(...)

if adapter_ok:
    logger.info("Job '%s': delivered ... via live adapter", job["id"], ...)
    delivered = True
```

- `cron/scheduler.py:808-810` returns `None` when no delivery errors were appended, so `mark_job_run(..., delivery_error=None)` records success.

## Impact

Jobs that deliver native attachments can silently lose the attachment while the scheduler reports successful delivery. For media-only jobs, generated reports, screenshots, audio, PDFs, or artifacts, this is a user-visible delivery failure hidden as success. Operators have to inspect logs to notice the problem, and automation cannot react via `last_delivery_error`.

## Proposed change

- Make `_send_media_via_adapter()` return a list of media delivery failures or raise a structured delivery exception.
- Append those failures to `_deliver_result()`'s `delivery_errors`.
- If text succeeds but one or more attachments fail, keep the execution status but set `last_delivery_error` with the attachment failure details.
- Optionally fallback to standalone `_send_to_platform(..., media_files=...)` when live-adapter media sending fails.

## Verification

- Add a fake live adapter whose text `send()` succeeds but media method returns `success=False` or raises.
- Run a cron job whose final response contains `MEDIA:/tmp/report.pdf`.
- Before the fix, the job has `delivery_error=None` despite failed media delivery.
- After the fix, the job records a delivery error that includes the failed media path/method.

items.title: API capabilities report jobs_admin false while authenticated cron-admin routes are enabled
items.body:
## Summary

The API server's `/v1/capabilities` response advertises `jobs_admin: False`, but the same server registers authenticated `/api/jobs` routes for listing, creating, updating, deleting, pausing/resuming, and running cron jobs. The advertised API trust surface does not match the enabled routes.

## Evidence

Local checkout: `/srv/platform/link_dot_hermes/hermes-agent`.

- `gateway/platforms/api_server.py:1069-1147` builds the `/v1/capabilities` response.
- `gateway/platforms/api_server.py:1114-1116` advertises:

```py
"admin_config_rw": False,
"jobs_admin": False,
"memory_write_api": False,
```

- `gateway/platforms/api_server.py:3085-3260` implements cron job management handlers, including list/create/get/update/delete/pause/resume/run operations guarded by `_check_auth()`.
- `gateway/platforms/api_server.py:4073-4081` registers the cron routes:

```py
GET    /api/jobs
POST   /api/jobs
GET    /api/jobs/{job_id}
PATCH  /api/jobs/{job_id}
DELETE /api/jobs/{job_id}
POST   /api/jobs/{job_id}/pause
POST   /api/jobs/{job_id}/resume
POST   /api/jobs/{job_id}/run
```

- `gateway/platforms/api_server.py:4103-4112` correctly requires an `API_SERVER_KEY`, so this is not unauthenticated access; it is a capability/authorization contract mismatch.

## Impact

Clients, dashboards, and deployment policies may rely on `/v1/capabilities` to decide what an API key can do. Advertising `jobs_admin: False` while enabling cron-admin routes can make a deployment appear safer than it is. Cron jobs can persist and execute future autonomous work, so this is a meaningful trust-boundary mismatch even though the routes are authenticated.

## Proposed change

Either:

1. Set `jobs_admin: True` whenever `/api/jobs` management routes are enabled; or
2. Add an explicit config flag/API scope for job administration and keep both the routes and capability disabled unless that flag/scope is present.

If the API key remains all-powerful, document that clearly and make `/v1/capabilities` reflect it.

## Verification

- Add API server tests asserting `/v1/capabilities` flags match route availability under the same config.
- When job routes are enabled, `jobs_admin` should be true.
- If a gating flag/scope is added, disabled routes should return 404/403 and `jobs_admin` should remain false.

items.title: Kanban review-column dispatch lacks a first-class transition path and references missing sdlc-review skill
items.body:
## Summary

The Kanban database defines a `review` status and a review dispatcher path, but normal task lifecycle code does not appear to provide a first-class transition into review. When a task is manually in review, the dispatcher assigns a hard-coded `sdlc-review` skill that does not appear to exist in the repo. This makes the autonomous review gate look available while being brittle or unreachable.

## Evidence

Local checkout: `/srv/platform/link_dot_hermes/hermes-agent`.

- `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:100` includes `review` as a valid status.
- `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:2632-2658` has `claim_review_task()`, which claims `review -> running` tasks.
- `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:5532-5536` comments describe a review-column workflow where workers move PR-ready tasks to `review`.
- `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:5541-5545` selects tasks with `status = 'review'` for review dispatch.
- `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:5578-5583` forces review dispatch to use `claimed.skills = ["sdlc-review"]`.
- `create_task()` only permits initial statuses from `VALID_INITIAL_STATUSES = {"running", "blocked"}` (`hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:100-101`, `1791-1794`), and ordinary creation maps statuses to `ready/todo/triage/blocked`, not `review` (`1889-1902`).
- `complete_task()` transitions `running|ready|blocked -> done`, not review (`hermes_cli/kanban_db.py:3076-3087`, `3147-3156`).
- Repo search found `sdlc-review` only in dispatcher comments/code/tests, not as a skill directory such as `skills/**/sdlc-review/SKILL.md`.

## Impact

For an autonomous engineering system, the review column is a governance gate: it should hold PR-ready work for independent verification before completion/merge. Today the code describes and dispatches that state, but workers do not appear to have a normal lifecycle operation to enter it, and reviewers are launched with a missing skill. The result is a review gate that can be skipped, require manual DB/status manipulation, or spawn under-instructed reviewers.

## Proposed change

- Add an explicit audited transition API/tool/CLI, for example `kanban_request_review(task_id, pr_url, summary, artifacts, reviewer_assignee?)`, that validates the current worker/task ownership and moves `running -> review`.
- Persist review metadata: PR URL, changed files, acceptance criteria evidence, originating run ID, and requested reviewer/assignee.
- Add the actual `sdlc-review` skill or change dispatch to load an existing review skill; fail closed if the configured review skill is missing.
- Add first-class reviewer outcomes:
  - approve -> `done` or configured completion transition,
  - reject -> `running` or `blocked` with review comments/reasons.

## Verification

- Tests for worker/tool/CLI transition from `running -> review`.
- Tests that review dispatch loads an existing review skill and refuses to dispatch when missing.
- Tests for approve/reject review outcomes and audit events.
- End-to-end test: worker opens/attaches PR -> requests review -> reviewer runs -> task transitions according to verdict.

items.title: [Bug]: Hermes Desktop shows generated local images as [Image blocked: ...] even though image generation succeeds

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
### Bug Description

Image generation succeeds and writes valid image files to the local Hermes cache, but Hermes Desktop renders the assistant’s markdown image as [Image blocked: alt text] when the image path is a Windows local filesystem path.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an image generation provider.
2. Ask Hermes Desktop to generate a simple image, for example: “Generate an image of a cute kitten.”
3. Wait for the image_generate tool to complete successfully.
4. Observe the assistant response in Desktop.

### Expected Behavior

The generated image should render inline in the chat UI, or the tool card should display/open the generated image.

### Actual Behavior

The UI displays something like:

`[Image` blocked: cute `kitten]`

The underlying image file exists locally and is valid.

items.title: [Bug]: Context compaction cross-contamination — cron session summaries leak into unrelated live conversations

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Description

After context compaction triggers, a compacted summary from a **cron job session** (unrelated, different platform) is injected into the current **live messaging session**, causing the agent to hallucinate and drift into an entirely different topic.

## Reproduction

1. Run a cron job that produces a session with compaction (e.g., a scheduled paper ingestion job)
2. In a separate live conversation (different platform, different topic), allow the conversation to reach a point where compaction triggers
3. Observe: the compacted summary injected contains content from the cron session, not just the current conversation

## Observed Behavior

The agent, after compaction, begins referencing topics, terminology, and context from the **unrelated cron session** — producing fabricated data and completely off-topic responses. The user perceives this as a sudden, unexplained topic shift.

## Expected Behavior

Compaction summaries should only contain context from the **current session**. Cross-session contamination should not occur. If compaction summaries are stored in a shared pool, they must be keyed/isolated by session ID.

## Impact

- Agent produces hallucinated, fabricated content derived from contaminated context
- Complete loss of user trust when the agent suddenly switches topics mid-conversation
- Particularly dangerous when cron sessions contain domain-specific content (finance, medicine, etc.) that pollutes unrelated conversations

## Suspected Root Cause

Compaction summaries may be stored/retrieved without proper session-level isolation, allowing a cron session's compacted summary to be injected into a live messaging session's context window.

## Related Issues

- #38392: compaction summaries injected as assistant messages (related: injection mechanism)
- #38364: compaction sections silently expand scope across conversations (related: cross-session scope leakage)
- #38763: session duplication from compaction (related: session lifecycle)

## Environment

- Hermes version: 0.15.x
- Platforms: feishu (live) + cron (scheduled)
- This bug is observed on a single Hermes instance running both gateway and cron scheduler

items.title: [Bug]: Windows hermes update fails when Gateway/Dashboard lock native .pyd dependencies

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows, `hermes update` can still fail even after the existing `hermes.exe` quarantine/concurrent-instance fixes, because long-running Hermes processes load native extension modules (`.pyd`) from the same venv. `uv pip install` then cannot remove/rename those loaded native modules.

This is a broader Windows self-update locking issue than the already-documented `hermes.exe` entry-point lock.

## Observed failure

Running `Hermes update` in PowerShell on Windows 10 with Gateway and Dashboard already running produced repeated dependency-install failures:

```text
→ Updating Python dependencies...
Using Python 3.11.14 environment at: venv
Resolved 104 packages in 653ms
      Built hermes-agent @ file:///C:/Users/lost/AppData/Local/hermes/hermes-agent
Prepared 1 package in 12.48s
error: failed to remove file
       C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\aiohttp/_http_parser.cp311-win_amd64.pyd:
       拒绝访问。 (os error 5)
  ⚠️ Optional extras failed, reinstalling base dependencies and retrying extras individually...
```

Later retries left the environment partially inconsistent and failed again while trying to install a pinned `aiohttp` wheel:

```text
warning: Failed to uninstall package at venv\Lib\site-packages\aiohttp-3.13.4.dist-info due to missing RECORD file. Installation may result in an incomplete environment.
Uninstalled 2 packages in 7ms
error: Failed to install: aiohttp-3.13.3-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl (aiohttp==3.13.3)
  Caused by: failed to rename file from
             C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\aiohttp\.tmpVgeWfu\_http_parser.cp311-win_amd64.pyd
             to C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\aiohttp\_http_parser.cp311-win_amd64.pyd:
             拒绝访问。 (os error 5)
```

## Running processes at the time

A process scan showed the active Hermes venv was simultaneously used by:

```text
C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main dashboard --port 9119 --no-open --skip-build
C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main gateway run
C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\hermes.exe update
C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\hermes.exe update
```

So the Gateway/Dashboard runtime likely had `aiohttp` loaded, and Windows refused to replace the loaded `.pyd` extension during `uv pip install`.

## Why this differs from existing Windows update issues

Existing reports/fixes such as #23327 and #26670 focus on `hermes.exe` / `hermes-gateway.exe` entry-point shim locking and concurrent `hermes.exe` instances.

This report is about native dependency modules loaded from the same venv, e.g.:

```text
venv\Lib\site-packages\aiohttp\_http_parser.cp311-win_amd64.pyd
```

Even if `hermes.exe` quarantine succeeds, `uv` can still fail when a long-running Gateway/Dashboard process has imported a native dependency from the venv.

## Expected behavior

On Windows, `hermes update` should either:

1. Refuse early with a clear message when any process is using the active Hermes venv, not only another `hermes.exe`; or preferably
2. Provide a safe update mode that handles the full lifecycle automatically.

Suggested UX:

```powershell
hermes update --safe
# or make this the default on Windows
```

Suggested safe-update flow:

1. Detect processes using the active Hermes venv, including:
   - Gateway (`hermes_cli.main gateway run`)
   - Dashboard (`hermes_cli.main dashboard ...`)
   - Desktop-spawned backend
   - open Hermes REPLs / CLI sessions
2. Spawn an external updater broker that does not depend on the venv being updated.
3. Stop Gateway/Dashboard/Desktop backend gracefully where possible.
4. Wait for `.exe` and `.pyd` locks to release.
5. Run the normal update.
6. Clear stale update/version cache if applicable.
7. Restart Gateway/Dashboard according to their previous running state.
8. Verify the result (`hermes --version`, `hermes gateway status`, Dashboard `/api/status` if it was running).

## Current workaround

Manual workaround:

```powershell
# Close Hermes Desktop and any open Hermes CLI/REPL first
hermes gateway stop
hermes dashboard --stop

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
  Where-Object {
    $_.CommandLine -like '*AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\venv*' -or
    $_.CommandLine -like '*hermes_cli.main*'
  } |
  ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force }

hermes update
hermes gateway start
hermes gateway status
```

This works, but it is too manual and easy for Windows users to get wrong. In the failed case above, the repeated optional-extra retry path also left `aiohttp` metadata partially inconsistent (`missing RECORD file`).

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Shell: PowerShell
- Hermes version during failure: `0.15.1`
- Python: `3.11.14`
- Install path: `C:\Users\lost\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent`
- Long-running processes: Gateway + Dashboard 9119

## Related

- #23327 — Windows `Access is denied (os error 5)` during update, focused on `hermes.exe`
- #26670 — concurrent Windows `hermes.exe` quarantine issue

This issue appears to be the next layer: loaded native dependency `.pyd` files from long-running Hermes processes.

items.title: bug: config migration (v25->v26) corrupts platform_toolsets, silently kills all tools

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Bug Description

During `hermes update` config format migration (v25 -> v26), the `platform_toolsets` section gets corrupted — the valid toolset name `hermes-cli` is rewritten to `hermes` (which doesn't exist), causing **all tools to silently stop working**.

## Root Cause

1. `resolve_toolset('hermes')` returns an empty list (because `hermes` is not a valid toolset name — `hermes-cli` is)
2. `all_tool_names` becomes empty → no configurable toolsets enabled
3. System prompt is built without any tool guidance
4. Model can only do text replies — zero tool calls

The failure is **silent**: no error, no warning, no log entry. The agent just stops using tools.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a working config with `platform_toolsets.cli: [hermes-cli]` and multiple platforms configured (telegram, discord, etc.)
2. Run `hermes update` when a config format version bump is available (v25 -> v26 in our case)
3. After migration, check `~/.hermes/config.yaml`

## Expected Behavior

- Config migration preserves valid toolset names (`hermes-cli`, not `hermes`)
- All platform toolsets remain intact (cli, telegram, discord, etc.)
- If migration encounters an unknown toolset name, it logs a warning

## Actual Behavior

- `hermes-cli` was changed to `hermes` (invalid)
- All platform toolsets except `cli` were stripped (telegram, discord, whatsapp, slack, signal, homeassistant, qqbot, yuanbao all gone)
- No error or warning logged
- Agent became a pure text-only assistant with 0 tool calls

## Evidence

**Before (backup from 2026-05-18):**

```yaml
platform_toolsets:
  cli:
  - hermes-cli
  telegram:
  - hermes-telegram
  discord:
  - hermes-discord
  whatsapp:
  - hermes-whatsapp
  slack:
  - hermes-slack
  # ... more platforms
```

**After migration (2026-06-02):**

```yaml
platform_toolsets:
  cli:
  - hermes  # <-- INVALID, should be hermes-cli
```

**Update log:**

```
ℹ Updating config format (v25 → v26)…
✓ Config format updated (no new settings to configure)
```

No warnings about the corrupted toolset names.

## Impact

- Agent completely loses ability to use tools (search, terminal, file ops, everything)
- No error message — user sees the agent respond with text only, may think it's a model issue
- Took significant debugging to trace back to the config migration

## Suggested Fix

1. Config migration should preserve existing toolset names verbatim — don't rename `hermes-cli` to `hermes`
2. After migration, validate all toolset names against `TOOLSETS` dict and warn on unknowns
3. Add a startup check: if `platform_toolsets` resolves to 0 tools, log a loud WARNING

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.5.1
- Hermes version: updated 2026-06-02
- Config format migration: v25 -> v26

items.title: Matrix adapter: room name not propagated to session source (shows generic user_name for all rooms)

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Problem

The Matrix adapter builds session sources without a `chat_name`. While WhatsApp and Telegram pass group/channel names to `build_source()` at ingestion, **Matrix omits it entirely**. Every room shows as the sender display name ("AVP") in `channel_directory.json` and session metadata, regardless of the actual Matrix room name set via `m.room.name`.

```
build_source(chat_id=room_id) → chat_name=None → fallback to user_name → "AVP"
```

This breaks domain-separated room workflows where each room has a distinct purpose (Home, Dev, Ops, Homeassistant, etc.) and the agent needs to know which room a message came from.

## Root cause

`_resolve_message_context()` in `matrix.py` never calls `get_chat_info()`, which already reads `m.room.name` from Matrix room state and returns the correct `{"name": "...", "type": "dm|group"}`. The data is available — just never wired through.

## Observed behavior

- All Matrix rooms appear as `AVP (dm)` in channel_directory.json
- Session origin data carries no room name
- Agent cannot distinguish which room a message originated from

## Expected behavior

Matrix adapter should match WhatsApp/Telegram pattern: resolve the room name at ingestion time and pass it to `build_source()`.

## Proposed fix

One added line in `_resolve_message_context()`. No new methods, no config files.

```diff
+        room_info = await self.get_chat_info(room_id)
         source = self.build_source(
             chat_id=room_id,
-            chat_type=chat_type,
+            chat_name=room_info["name"],
+            chat_type=room_info["type"],
```

`get_chat_info()` (line 1147) already exists, reads `m.room.name`, and returns `{"name": "Homeassistant", "type": "dm"}`. The fix just calls it.

## Design consistency

| Adapter | `chat_name` source |
|---|---|
| WhatsApp | `data.get("chatName")` |
| Telegram | `chat.title` |
| Matrix (current) | *(omitted — None)* |
| Matrix (fixed) | `get_chat_info()` → `m.room.name` |

## Impact

- `sessions.json` origin data carries actual Matrix room name
- `channel_directory.json` displays room names instead of "AVP"
- No downstream consumers need changes
- No new I/O — `get_chat_info()` already used elsewhere in the adapter

items.title: Proposal: OpenTelemetry (OTEL) trace emitter plugin

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
## Motivation

Hermes Agent is a powerful AI coding orchestrator, but it lacks built-in observability. Users currently have no structured way to:
- View session timelines
- Inspect tool call spans
- Debug prompt/response flows
- Measure performance across runs

## Proposal

Add an **OTEL (OpenTelemetry) exporter plugin** to Hermes Agent that emits traces for every session, tool call, LLM call, and cron job.

### Scope (Phase 1)
- OTLP HTTP exporter (push to any OTEL-compatible backend)
- Span types: session, tool, model, cron
- Config via `hermes config` (otel.enabled, otel.endpoint, otel.headers)
- Graceful degradation if endpoint unreachable

### Why OTEL?
- Vendor-neutral — works with Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb, or any OTLP-compatible viewer
- Industry standard — no lock-in
- Can be consumed by any OTEL-compatible frontend

### Out of scope (Phase 1)
- Full observability dashboard
- Agent-level metrics (statsd/prometheus)
- Streaming traces

## References
- OTEL semantic conventions: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Environment
- macOS 26.2 (beta)
- Hermes v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)
- Hermes Desktop App (Electron, bundled)
- Chinese (Simplified) input method (IME)

## Symptom
When typing Chinese characters in the Desktop App input box using the native macOS Chinese IME:
1. Type Chinese characters (e.g. pinyin) → IME candidate window appears
2. Press Enter to confirm and submit the message
3. **Result**: Only symbols/prefix characters are sent, Chinese text is lost
4. Workaround: Press Shift+Enter instead — works correctly

This means Chinese-speaking users cannot use the normal Enter key to send messages. They must remember to use Shift+Enter every time, which is non-standard and frustrating.

## Expected Behavior
- Pressing Enter should: (1) confirm IME composition, (2) submit the full message text
- This is the standard behavior in all native chat apps (WeChat, Telegram, etc.)
- Shift+Enter should insert a newline (which currently works)

## Likely Cause
The Enter key event handler in the chat input field does not properly wait for `compositionend` event from the IME before submitting. When the IME is active, pressing Enter fires a `keydown` event before the IME has finished composing the text, causing the app to submit an incomplete string.

Standard fix: check `event.isComposing` or `event.keyCode === 229` (Windows) / handle `compositionend` event properly on macOS.

## Impact
- Breaks the app for all CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) users
- These users are forced to use CLI, gateway channels, or Shift+Enter workaround
- May affect other IME-based languages (Japanese Kana/Kanji, Korean Hangul)

## Workaround (for users)
Press Shift+Enter instead of Enter to submit messages.
